newsitem.title: USA: Chase wins Reuters quarterly U.S. forecast survey.
newsitem.headline: Chase wins Reuters quarterly U.S. forecast survey.

text.p: Chase Securities Inc topped several other U.S. firms in forecasting three key economic data points in a Reuters quarterly survey.
In the July poll, 23 economists and analysts forecast economic indicators, interest rates and foreign exchange rates up to eight quarters ahead.
Chase edged out seven other prognosticators who offered projections for second-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and the end-of-September 30-year Treasury bond yield and dollar/mark exchange rate.

Chase averaged 94.88 percent accuracy in those three components of the Reuters poll. DRI/McGraw Hill was nearly as accurate, at 94.52 percent. Daiwa Securities America Inc was a close third, with 94.09 percent accuracy.
"What we were thinking at the time was that the economy would slow down gradually but was still rapid," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
The third quarter tossed economists a few curves, said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa.
"The surprise in the third quarter was how soft consumer spending was," Moran said. "The second (surprise) was the widening of the trade deficit."
Individually, Chase's forecast of a 4.4 percent annual GDP growth rate in the second quarter most closely matched actual GDP growth of a surprising 4.7 percent.
PaineWebber Group Inc made the second-place forecast of 4.3 percent, and the Georgia State University economic forecasting center came in third with a projection of 4.2 percent.
Although Chase outguessed everyone on GDP, other survey participants topped the bond yield and exchange rate categories.

The 30-year Treasury bond closed out the third quarter with a 6.92 percent yield, just a touch higher than WEFA Group's pick of 6.90 percent. The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp (FHLMC or Freddie Mac) provided a similarly prescient forecast of 6.85 percent.

Forecasting the dollar/mark exchange rate, Daiwa and Northern Trust Co outshone other firms with their forecast of 1.5300 marks, just off the actual September 30 London close of 1.5260 marks. They tied for first place in that category.
Georgia State took second with a prediction of 1.5330.

For certain key economic elements, economists' long-range expectations changed little over the past three months. In the Reuters quarterly U.S. economic survey conducted last week and released this Thursday, experts' GDP and bond-yield forecasts showed a pattern similar to that of the July poll.
Prognosticators again said GDP would slow to below 3.0 percent year-on-year for 1996 and to near 2.0 percent for 1997. They forecast the 30-year bond yield would sink gradually from current levels.
"There's a difference between what we were thinking then and what we're thinking now," said Chase's Glassman.
Three months ago economists were predicting higher short-term interest rates, but now they expect the central bank to remain neutral in the near term, he said.
"We thought the Fed would be tightening in response to the declining unemployment rate," Glassman said.
